source.title: Assessment of Aquatic Biodiversity in Rice-based Ecosystems in Selected Sites in Luzon, the Philippines
source.citation: Abella TA, Halwart M, Velasco RR, Newingham MCV, Paredes JC, Lanuza EC, Reyes RA, Vera Cruz EM. 2014. In: Halwart M, Bartley D, Bueno PB, Innes-Taylor N (eds.), Aquatic Biodiversity in Rice-based Ecosystems: Studies and Reports from Indonesia, Lao PDR and the Philippines. FAO, Rome, pp. 44-58. ISBN 978-92-5-108414-4.
source.access: The FAO-hosted full PDF was retrieved over HTTPS and hash-checked. Its page text extraction was not machine-readable in this environment; detailed chapter text was cross-read in an openly displayed full-text copy of the same titled FAO volume. No PDF was committed to the repository.

rights.publisherTerms: The volume states that FAO encourages reproduction for private study, research, teaching, and non-commercial products/services with acknowledgement. Translation, adaptation, resale and other commercial uses require a rights request.
rights.decision: Retain minimal attributed research facts only. Confirm that any future app use remains within the non-commercial permission or obtain applicable permission before public publication; do not reproduce the chapter's text, tables, figures or photos.

site.name: Talampas village, Bustos, Bulacan
site.waterInfrastructureContext: The chapter says large National Irrigation Administration AMRIS tributary channels pass through Talampas and provide aquatic food resources to residents.
site.scopeLimit: This is a village/site-level rice-based ecosystem assessment. It is not a fish inventory for Bustos Dam, Angat Dam, the entire Angat River, or all Bulacan waters. The chapter gives no exact canal names, station coordinates, or study polygon for Talampas.

methods.design: Assessment of aquatic organisms used as food by local residents; site reconnaissance, interviews, repeated visits to target sites, field observations, and photo documentation.
methods.visitFrequency: The authors say the sites were visited at least three times weekly during the study.
methods.selectionRule: Only species taken out of the water by users for food were recorded; intentional sampling was avoided.
methods.identification: The authors say identifications used CLSU biological-science, Freshwater Aquaculture Center, and BFAR facilities; photographs were sent to Peter Balzer via FAO for confirmation.
limitations: No voucher or collection/catalog number is reported for the Talampas fishes.
No exact observation date is given for an individual taxon; September-December 2013 is the study period.
The observations document historical site use/capture, not present-day occurrence, abundance, catchability, food safety, or legal permission.
The account does not resolve whether each fish was wild, escaped from culture, or stocked at the individual observation level.

sourceConflicts: The chapter lists eight fish entries, but includes genus-only and common-name-only entries; this review does not treat the eight rows as eight resolved species.
The account names Cyprinus sp. Silap and also lists Karpa without a scientific name; possible overlap is unresolved and they are not counted as distinct taxa.
A paragraph links biya abundance to proximity to Bustos Dam, while the summary links it to Angat Dam. No dam-specific species assertion is made from this conflict.
The text reports Tilapia nilotica and identifies the name as Oreochromis niloticus through the current Catalog of Fishes; this is a name mapping, not a re-identification of archived specimens.
nextStep: Seek a distinct fish-specific survey for Angat/Bustos reservoirs or named Bulacan rivers, then review Talampas source rights and the historical-site scope before any public projection. Keep fishpond/aquaculture production, rice-field catches, reservoir waters, and river reaches as different evidence contexts.
